question_text: A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. He is a 35-pack-year smoker. His blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg. His BMI is 37 kg/m2. Oropharyngeal examination shows a small orifice and an enlarged tongue and uvula. The soft palate is low-lying. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. He is a 35-pack-year smoker. His blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg. His BMI is 37 kg/m2. Oropharyngeal examination shows a small orifice and an enlarged tongue and uvula. The soft palate is low-lying. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
opb. Heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction
opc. Idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension
opd. Obstructive sleep apnea
ope. Pulmonary thromboembolism

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with increasing dyspnea, lower extremity swelling, excessive daytime sleepiness, and signs of upper airway obstruction (enlarged tongue and uvula, low-lying soft palate). These findings are consistent with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which can lead to hypoxia during sleep, frequent awakenings, and excessive daytime sleepiness. The elevated blood pressure and mildly dilated right ventricle with elevated pulmonary artery pressure further support the diagnosis of OSA, as it can cause pulmonary hypertension due to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. The absence of cough and clear lung auscultation make chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) less likely. The echocardiography findings and the ventilation-perfusion scan showing no abnormalities also reduce the likelihood of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and pulmonary thromboembolism. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is obstructive sleep apnea.
